title: Beyond GDP: Can Happiness Be Measured?
subtitle: Governments are increasingly interested in how their citizens feel. The data may not bear the weight now being placed on it.

paragraphs.text: When the economist Simon Kuznets presented the first official estimates of national income to the US Congress in 1934, he attached a caveat: the welfare of a nation, he wrote, could scarcely be inferred from a measurement of its income. The warning went largely unheeded. Within a generation, gross domestic product had become the master statistic of public life, the figure by which governments were judged and countries ranked. That a number designed to track the volume of market transactions should have come to stand for national success is one of the stranger accidents of modern history.

Its shortcomings are by now familiar. GDP counts the clearing up after a disaster as a contribution to output, yet ignores the unpaid labour of parents and carers. It is silent about how income is distributed, so that an economy can expand while most of its citizens become no better off. Above all, it measures means rather than ends: people want income not for its own sake but for the lives it makes possible. Small wonder, then, that researchers and politicians have proposed simply asking people how their lives are going.

The idea has a respectable pedigree. In the 1970s the King of Bhutan declared that Gross National Happiness mattered more than Gross National Product, a principle the kingdom later turned into a formal index. In 2009 a commission set up by the French government urged statistical offices to give far greater weight to wellbeing. Shortly afterwards, Britain's Office for National Statistics began asking a large sample of adults four questions every year, among them how satisfied they were with their lives, with answers given on a scale from nought to ten. Since 2012 the World Happiness Report has ranked countries on comparable survey data, and in 2019 New Zealand presented what it called a 'wellbeing budget', in which spending priorities were justified by their expected effect on citizens' quality of life rather than on growth alone.

The case for such measures is not merely sentimental. Self-reported wellbeing turns out to be surprisingly consistent with other evidence: people who call themselves satisfied with their lives are more likely to be judged happy by their friends and, according to some studies, tend to live longer. Surveys have also revealed patterns invisible to conventional economics. Unemployment, for instance, depresses life satisfaction far more than the loss of income alone would predict, and the damage can persist long after a person has found new work. Loneliness, long commutes and chronic pain all weigh more heavily in people's assessments of their lives than modest differences in income. If governments care about such things, they ought to measure them.

Yet the methodological difficulties are considerable, and enthusiasts tend to underestimate them. The first concerns the scale itself. When one person reports a seven and another an eight, there is no guarantee that they mean the same thing; cultural norms about how positively one ought to describe one's own life vary widely, so international league tables may partly be measuring differences in modesty rather than in contentment. The second is that answers are sensitive to context. In one experiment, people questioned on sunny days reported greater satisfaction than those questioned on rainy ones; in another, asking respondents about their romantic lives immediately before the general question noticeably altered their answers. Such distortions largely cancel out in large samples, but make small year-on-year changes hazardous to interpret.

A deeper problem is adaptation. Human beings are remarkably adept at adjusting their expectations to their circumstances, and a scale that runs from nought to ten has a ceiling that income does not. This helps to explain the puzzle, identified in the 1970s by the economist Richard Easterlin, that average reported happiness in a number of wealthy countries barely rose over decades in which incomes multiplied. Some have concluded that growth is therefore futile. That conclusion does not follow. A population that has grown accustomed to clean water, antibiotics and central heating may report the same score as its grandparents, but it would be perverse to claim that nothing had improved. A measure incapable of registering such gains is at best an incomplete guide to progress.

There is also a political hazard. A single wellbeing figure is, if anything, more open to manipulation than GDP, because it depends on how questions are worded, when they are asked and which of many possible indicators is promoted to the headline. Dr Miriam Hale, a statistician who advises governments on survey design, observes that the more weight a number is made to carry, the stronger the temptation to improve the number rather than the reality it is meant to reflect. A government that judged itself by average life satisfaction might also be tempted to neglect minorities whose suffering barely moves the national mean.

None of this means abandoning the project. The argument for looking beyond GDP is overwhelming; the error lies in searching for a replacement that does the same job. What wellbeing data does well is to draw attention to neglected sources of misery - mental illness, isolation, insecure work - and to test whether particular policies actually make people's lives better. What it cannot do is compress the many dimensions of a good society into a single figure for politicians to chase. The sensible course is a dashboard rather than a scoreboard: a small set of indicators covering income, health, the environment and people's own assessments of their lives, each read alongside the others. Kuznets, who distrusted single numbers, would surely have approved.

items.statement: It is odd that GDP came to be regarded as the main indicator of how well a country is doing.
items.evidence: That a number designed to track the volume of market transactions should have come to stand for national success is one of the stranger accidents of modern history.

items.statement: Bhutan's approach to measuring happiness has been more effective than Britain's.
items.note: The writer describes both Bhutan's index and the ONS questions but never compares how well either has worked.

items.statement: What people say about their own wellbeing cannot be trusted, as it conflicts with other kinds of evidence.
items.evidence: Self-reported wellbeing turns out to be surprisingly consistent with other evidence
items.note: The writer says self-reports agree with other evidence - the opposite of the statement.

items.statement: The fact that reported happiness has hardly increased in some wealthy countries proves that economic growth has brought no real benefit.
items.evidence: Some have concluded that growth is therefore futile. That conclusion does not follow.
items.note: The writer reports this view only in order to reject it.

items.statement: Wellbeing data can be useful in judging whether specific government measures improve people's lives.
items.evidence: What wellbeing data does well is to draw attention to neglected sources of misery - mental illness, isolation, insecure work - and to test whether particular policies actually make people's lives better.

items.stem: Why does the writer mention 'the clearing up after a disaster' in the second paragraph?
options: to show that GDP can increase as a result of events that harm people
to argue that governments should spend more on emergency services
to illustrate how GDP overlooks work that is not paid for
to suggest that natural disasters reduce a country's economic output
items.evidence: GDP counts the clearing up after a disaster as a contribution to output
items.note: C borrows 'unpaid labour' from the same sentence, but that is a separate shortcoming; D reverses the point, since the clean-up adds to output.

items.stem: What does the writer say about New Zealand's 2019 budget?
options: It was the first budget to abandon economic growth as a goal.
It relied on survey data published in the World Happiness Report.
It explained spending decisions in terms of their likely impact on quality of life.
It followed the recommendations of the commission set up in France.
items.evidence: in which spending priorities were justified by their expected effect on citizens' quality of life rather than on growth alone
items.note: A is a trap: 'rather than on growth alone' means growth was still considered, not abandoned.

items.stem: According to the fifth paragraph, international comparisons of happiness may be unreliable because
options: surveys are carried out in different weather conditions in different countries.
people from different cultures vary in how favourably they feel they should describe their lives.
the samples used in some countries are too small to be meaningful.
respondents are asked about their romantic lives before the main question.
items.evidence: cultural norms about how positively one ought to describe one's own life vary widely, so international league tables may partly be measuring differences in modesty rather than in contentment
items.note: A and D distort the two experiments, which concern context effects on individuals, not international rankings; sample size (C) is said to reduce distortion, not cause it.

items.stem: What point does Dr Miriam Hale make?
options: Wellbeing surveys are more costly to run than governments realise.
Survey questions should be worded in the same way in every country.
Minority groups are frequently left out of national surveys.
Giving a statistic great importance encourages efforts to change the figure instead of the situation.
items.evidence: the more weight a number is made to carry, the stronger the temptation to improve the number rather than the reality it is meant to reflect
items.note: C echoes the writer's own next sentence about minorities, which is about neglect in policy, not exclusion from surveys, and is not Hale's point.

groups.title: The limits of wellbeing measures
lines: Because people show a great capacity for {1}, and because a wellbeing scale has a fixed upper limit, average scores in some rich countries have remained largely {2} even as incomes have risen dramatically. This, however, does not prove that life has not got better. Wellbeing figures are also vulnerable to {3}, since the results depend on how and when questions are asked. The writer concludes that such data is most valuable for highlighting {4} problems, and recommends using a {5} of indicators rather than a single headline figure.

answers.evidence: Human beings are remarkably adept at adjusting their expectations to their circumstances
average reported happiness in a number of wealthy countries barely rose over decades in which incomes multiplied
A single wellbeing figure is, if anything, more open to manipulation than GDP, because it depends on how questions are worded, when they are asked
draw attention to neglected sources of misery
a small set of indicators covering income, health, the environment and people's own assessments of their lives, each read alongside the others
